claim: MES-4 is a C. elegans H3K36 methyltransferase that is essential for germline survival and development in offspring.
source: A premier example is the Caenorhabditis elegans H3K36 methyltransferase MES-4, which is essential for germline survival and development in offspring.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about MES-4.

claim: mes-4 nascent germlines displayed downregulation of some germline genes.
source: mes-4 nascent germlines displayed downregulation of some germline genes, upregulation of some somatic genes, and dramatic upregulation of hundreds of genes on the X chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data from dissected nascent germlines presented in the manuscript.

claim: mes-4 nascent germlines displayed upregulation of some somatic genes.
source: mes-4 nascent germlines displayed downregulation of some germline genes, upregulation of some somatic genes, and dramatic upregulation of hundreds of genes on the X chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data from dissected nascent germlines presented in the manuscript.

claim: mes-4 nascent germlines displayed dramatic upregulation of hundreds of genes on the X chromosome.
source: mes-4 nascent germlines displayed downregulation of some germline genes, upregulation of some somatic genes, and dramatic upregulation of hundreds of genes on the X chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data from dissected nascent germlines presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upregulation of one or more genes on the X is the cause of germline death in mes-4 mutants.
source: We demonstrated that upregulation of one or more genes on the X is the cause of germline death by generating and analyzing mes-4 mutants that inherited different endowments of X chromosome(s).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments analyzing mes-4 mutants with different X-chromosome inheritance patterns.

claim: Removal of the THAP transcription factor LIN-15B from mes-4 mutants reduced X misexpression.
source: Intriguingly, removal of the THAP transcription factor LIN-15B from mes-4 mutants reduced X misexpression and prevented germline death.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing mes-4; lin-15B double mutants to mes-4 single mutants.

claim: Removal of LIN-15B from mes-4 mutants prevented germline death.
source: Intriguingly, removal of the THAP transcription factor LIN-15B from mes-4 mutants reduced X misexpression and prevented germline death.
evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis of mes-4; lin-15B double mutants.

claim: lin-15B is X-linked.
source: lin-15B is X-linked and misexpressed in mes-4 PGCs, identifying it as a critical target for MES-4 repression.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic location of lin-15B.

claim: lin-15B is misexpressed in mes-4 PGCs.
source: lin-15B is X-linked and misexpressed in mes-4 PGCs, identifying it as a critical target for MES-4 repression.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and smFISH data showing upregulation of lin-15B in mes-4 PGCs.

claim: lin-15B is a critical target for MES-4 repression.
source: lin-15B is X-linked and misexpressed in mes-4 PGCs, identifying it as a critical target for MES-4 repression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that lin-15B is upregulated in mes-4 mutants and its removal rescues germline death.

claim: The findings about MES-4 extend to the H3K27 methyltransferase MES-2/3/6 (PRC2).
source: The above findings extend to the H3K27 methyltransferase MES-2/3/6, the C. elegans version of polycomb repressive complex 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by similar transcriptome and genetic analyses performed on mes-3 (PRC2 component) mutants.

claim: Maternal MES-4 and PRC2 cooperate to protect germline survival by preventing synthesis of germline-toxic products encoded by genes on the X chromosome, including the key transcription factor LIN-15B.
source: We propose that maternal MES-4 and PRC2 cooperate to protect germline survival by preventing synthesis of germline-toxic products encoded by genes on the X chromosome, including the key transcription factor LIN-15B.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined findings from mes-4 and mes-3 mutant analyses.

claim: MES-2, MES-3, and MES-6 assemble into a trimeric complex that is the C. elegans version of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2).
source: MES-2, MES-3, and MES-6 assemble into a trimeric complex that is the C. elegans version of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) (Xu et al., 2001; Bender et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PRC2 is a histone methyltransferase (HMT) that methylates Lys 27 on histone H3 (H3K27me) to repress genes.
source: PRC2 is a histone methyltransferase (HMT) that methylates Lys 27 on histone H3 (H3K27me) to repress genes that are packaged by those methylated nucleosomes (Ketel et al., 2005; Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Pengelly et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MES-4 is an HMT that methylates Lys 36 on H3 (H3K36me).
source: MES-4 is an HMT that methylates Lys 36 on H3 (H3K36me), which marks actively transcribed genes and has context-dependent roles in transcriptional regulation (Bender et al., 2006; Furuhashi et al., 2010; Rechtsteiner et al., 2010; Kreher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: H3K36me marks actively transcribed genes and has context-dependent roles in transcriptional regulation.
source: MES-4 is an HMT that methylates Lys 36 on H3 (H3K36me), which marks actively transcribed genes and has context-dependent roles in transcriptional regulation (Bender et al., 2006; Furuhashi et al., 2010; Rechtsteiner et al., 2010; Kreher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of either PRC2 or MES-4 causes nearly identical mutant phenotypes.
source: Although PRC2 and MES-4 catalyze opposing flavors of histone marking, the loss of either causes nearly identical mutant phenotypes (Capowski et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Worms that inherit a maternal load of MES-4 gene product but cannot synthesize zygotic product (mes M+Z- mutants) are fertile.
source: Worms that inherit a maternal load of gene product but cannot synthesize zygotic product (referred to as mes M+Z- mutants) are fertile.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous genetic studies.

claim: Worms that do not inherit a maternal load or produce zygotic MES-4 gene product (mes M-Z- mutants) are sterile due to death of nascent germ cells in early- to mid-stage larvae.
source: Worms that do not inherit a maternal load or produce zygotic gene product (mes M-Z- mutants) are sterile due to death of nascent germ cells in early- to mid-stage larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous genetic studies.

claim: In mes M-Z+ mutants, zygotically synthesized MES-4 product does not rescue fertility.
source: In mes M-Z+ mutants, zygotically synthesized product does not rescue fertility, highlighting the critical importance of maternal product.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous genetic studies.

claim: Among mes-4 M-Z- mutants, hermaphrodites (with two X chromosomes) are always sterile, while males (with one X chromosome) can be fertile.
source: First, among mes-4 M-Z- mutants, hermaphrodites (with two X chromosomes) are always sterile, while males (with one X chromosome) can be fertile (Garvin et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Profiling transcripts in the germlines of fertile mes-4 M+Z- mutant hermaphrodites revealed that the most dramatic effect of losing zygotic MES-4 is upregulation of genes on the X.
source: Second, profiling transcripts in the germlines of fertile mes-4 M+Z- mutant hermaphrodites revealed that the most dramatic effect of losing zygotic MES-4 is upregulation of genes on the X (Bender et al., 2006; Gaydos et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The X chromosomes are normally kept globally repressed during all stages of germline development in males and during most stages of germline development in hermaphrodites.
source: Notably, the X chromosomes are normally kept globally repressed during all stages of germline development in males and during most stages of germline development in hermaphrodites (Kelly et al., 2002; Reinke et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2009; Arico et al., 2011; Strome et al., 2014; Tzur et al., 2018), and likely as a consequence, most germline-expressed genes are located on the autosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most germline-expressed genes are located on the autosomes.
source: Notably, the X chromosomes are normally kept globally repressed during all stages of germline development in males and during most stages of germline development in hermaphrodites (Kelly et al., 2002; Reinke et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2009; Arico et al., 2011; Strome et al., 2014; Tzur et al., 2018), and likely as a consequence, most germline-expressed genes are located on the autosomes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that X chromosomes are repressed in the germline.

claim: 176 genes were significantly downregulated in mes-4 mutant PGCs compared to wild-type PGCs.
source: Our analysis identified 176 DOWN genes and 450 UP genes (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 450 genes were significantly upregulated in mes-4 mutant PGCs compared to wild-type PGCs.
source: Our analysis identified 176 DOWN genes and 450 UP genes (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 6 of 168 germline-specific genes (4%) are significantly downregulated in mes-4 PGCs.
source: We found that some germline-specific genes (6 of 168 genes, or 4%), germline-enriched genes (65 of 2176 genes, or 3%), and MES-4-bound genes (124 of 4132, or 3%) are significantly DOWN in mes-4 PGCs (Figure 1B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 65 of 2176 germline-enriched genes (3%) are significantly downregulated in mes-4 PGCs.
source: We found that some germline-specific genes (6 of 168 genes, or 4%), germline-enriched genes (65 of 2176 genes, or 3%), and MES-4-bound genes (124 of 4132, or 3%) are significantly DOWN in mes-4 PGCs (Figure 1B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 124 of 4132 MES-4-bound genes (3%) are significantly downregulated in mes-4 PGCs.
source: We found that some germline-specific genes (6 of 168 genes, or 4%), germline-enriched genes (65 of 2176 genes, or 3%), and MES-4-bound genes (124 of 4132, or 3%) are significantly DOWN in mes-4 PGCs (Figure 1B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The numbers of downregulated genes for each germline gene set in mes-4 PGCs are not more than expected by chance.
source: However, the numbers of DOWN genes for each gene set are not more than expected by chance (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by hypergeometric tests shown in Figure 1E.

claim: mes-4 EGCs downregulated 21 of 168 germline-specific genes (13%).
source: We found that mes-4 EGCs downregulated more germline-specific genes (21 of 168, or 13%), more germline-enriched genes (247 of 2176, or 11%), and more MES-4-bound genes (396 of 4132, or 10%) than mes-4 PGCs (Figure 2A, D and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: mes-4 EGCs downregulated 247 of 2176 germline-enriched genes (11%).
source: We found that mes-4 EGCs downregulated more germline-specific genes (21 of 168, or 13%), more germline-enriched genes (247 of 2176, or 11%), and more MES-4-bound genes (396 of 4132, or 10%) than mes-4 PGCs (Figure 2A, D and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: mes-4 EGCs downregulated 396 of 4132 MES-4-bound genes (10%).
source: We found that mes-4 EGCs downregulated more germline-specific genes (21 of 168, or 13%), more germline-enriched genes (247 of 2176, or 11%), and more MES-4-bound genes (396 of 4132, or 10%) than mes-4 PGCs (Figure 2A, D and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The numbers of downregulated genes for each germline gene set in mes-4 EGCs are more than expected by chance.
source: The numbers of DOWN genes for each gene set are more than expected by chance (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by hypergeometric tests shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The transcript abundance of cpg-2 was significantly lower in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs by smFISH analysis.
source: Corroborating our RNA-seq analysis, smFISH analysis showed that the transcript abundance of cpg-2 was significantly lower in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs, while the transcript abundance of pgl-3 was not significantly different (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The transcript abundance of pgl-3 was not significantly different between mes-4 and wt PGCs by smFISH analysis.
source: Corroborating our RNA-seq analysis, smFISH analysis showed that the transcript abundance of cpg-2 was significantly lower in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs, while the transcript abundance of pgl-3 was not significantly different (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: mes-4 nascent germ cells fail to normally express a small number of germline genes, but display near-normal expression of the majority of germline genes analyzed.
source: Together, our RNA-seq and smFISH analysis showed that mes-4 nascent germ cells fail to normally express a small number of germline genes, but display near-normal expression of the majority of germline genes analyzed.
evidence: This claim is supported by combined RNA-seq and smFISH data.

claim: 19 upregulated genes in mes-4 PGCs are soma-specific.
source: We found that 19 and 64 UP genes in mes-4 PGCs and mes-4 EGCs, respectively, are soma-specific, the latter of which is a higher number than expected by chance (Figure 1C and F, Figure 2B, E and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: 64 upregulated genes in mes-4 EGCs are soma-specific, which is a higher number than expected by chance.
source: We found that 19 and 64 UP genes in mes-4 PGCs and mes-4 EGCs, respectively, are soma-specific, the latter of which is a higher number than expected by chance (Figure 1C and F, Figure 2B, E and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data and hypergeometric tests shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: mes-4 germ cells begin to inappropriately express some somatic genes as they age.
source: We conclude that mes-4 germ cells begin to inappropriately express some somatic genes as they age.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that more soma-specific genes are upregulated in EGCs than in PGCs.

claim: 311 of the 2808 (11%) protein-coding X genes were upregulated in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs.
source: We found that 311 of the 2808 (11%) protein-coding X genes were UP in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: More than half of all upregulated genes in mes-4 PGCs are on the X chromosome (311 out of 450 genes), which is significantly higher than expected by chance.
source: Strikingly, more than half of all UP genes are on the X chromosome (311 out of 450 genes), and this number is significantly higher than expected by chance (Figure 1D and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and hypergeometric tests shown in Figure 1.

claim: mes-4 EGCs misexpressed 568 X genes, including almost all of the X genes that were misexpressed in mes-4 PGCs and an additional 273 X genes.
source: mes-4 EGCs misexpressed 568 X genes, including almost all of the X genes that were misexpressed in mes-4 PGCs and an additional 273 X genes (Figure 2C, F and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: mes-4 PGCs misexpress many genes on the X chromosome and X misexpression becomes more severe in their descendant EGCs.
source: These data show that mes-4 PGCs misexpress many genes on the X chromosome and that X misexpression becomes more severe in their descendant EGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing PGCs and EGCs.

claim: All four X genes tested by smFISH had higher transcript abundance in mes-4 PGCs than in wt PGCs.
source: smFISH analysis showed that all four X genes had higher transcript abundance in mes-4 PGCs than in wt PGCs (Figure 3D–F), corroborating our transcriptome analysis (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The X chromosome is the primary focus of MES-4 regulation in PGCs.
source: These data reveal that the X chromosome is the primary focus of MES-4 regulation in PGCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that X genes are the most dramatically misregulated in mes-4 PGCs.

claim: All live-imaged mes-4 mutant hermaphrodites lacked a germline.
source: All live-imaged mes-4 mutant hermaphrodites lacked a germline (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 21% of mes-4 mutant Xoo males had a partial germline and 4% had a full germline.
source: In contrast, some mes-4 mutant males that inherited their single X from an oocyte (Xoo males) had either a partial or full germline (21 and 4%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 67% of him-8; mes-4 mutant Xsp males made full germlines compared to only 4% of mes-4 mutant Xoo males.
source: Strikingly, 67% of him-8; mes-4 mutant Xsp males made full germlines compared to only 4% of mes-4 mutant Xoo males.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All mes-4 mutant XooXoo hermaphrodites lacked a germline.
source: While all mes-4 mutant XooXoo hermaphrodites lacked a germline, some mes-4 mutant XspXsp hermaphrodites had a partial or full germline (32 and 18%, respectively) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 32% of mes-4 mutant XspXsp hermaphrodites had a partial germline and 18% had a full germline.
source: While all mes-4 mutant XooXoo hermaphrodites lacked a germline, some mes-4 mutant XspXsp hermaphrodites had a partial or full germline (32 and 18%, respectively) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Misexpression of one or more X genes causes germline death in mes-4 mutants.
source: Our combined genetic analysis demonstrates that misexpression of one or more X genes causes germline death in mes-4 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments showing that X-chromosome dosage and inheritance pattern affect germline health in mes-4 mutants.

claim: mes-4 mutant PGCs can launch a transcription program that supports germline development.
source: It also underscores that mes-4 mutant PGCs can launch a transcription program that supports germline development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that some mes-4 mutants with specific X-chromosome inheritance patterns can develop full germlines.

claim: Over half (57%) of F1 adult offspring had a full germline if their PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from the sperm and maternal MES-4.
source: We found that over half (57%) of F1 adult offspring had a full germline if their PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from the sperm and maternal MES-4 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 0% of F1 adult offspring had a full germline if their PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from the sperm and did not inherit maternal MES-4.
source: In contrast, 0% of F1 adult offspring had a full germline if their PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from the sperm and did not inherit maternal MES-4 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Maternally loaded MES-4 is critical for offspring germline development, but its critical role is not to transmit H3K36me3 patterns from parents to offspring.
source: This result shows that maternally loaded MES-4 is critical for offspring germline development, but that its critical role is not to transmit H3K36me3 patterns from parents to offspring.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that offspring can develop germlines even when inheriting H3K36me3(-) chromosomes, as long as they have maternal MES-4.

claim: MES-4 cannot catalyze de novo H3K36me3 marking on H3K36me3(-) chromosomes.
source: MES-4 cannot catalyze de novo H3K36me3 marking on H3K36me3(-) chromosomes, but the other H3K36 HMT, MET-1, can do so in response to transcriptional turn-on, like H3K36 HMTs in other species (Furuhashi et al., 2010; Kreher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MET-1 can catalyze de novo H3K36me3 marking on H3K36me3(-) chromosomes in response to transcriptional turn-on.
source: MES-4 cannot catalyze de novo H3K36me3 marking on H3K36me3(-) chromosomes, but the other H3K36 HMT, MET-1, can do so in response to transcriptional turn-on, like H3K36 HMTs in other species (Furuhashi et al., 2010; Kreher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Removal of maternal MET-1 caused almost all F1 offspring whose PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from sperm to lack a germline.
source: We found that removal of maternal MET-1 caused almost all F1 offspring whose PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from sperm to lack a germline.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Maternal loads of both H3K36 HMTs (MES-4 and MET-1) are required for F1 offspring whose PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from sperm to make a germline.
source: Therefore, maternal loads of both H3K36 HMTs are required for F1 offspring whose PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from sperm to make a germline.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Newly established H3K36me3 marking of H3K36me3(-) chromosomes by maternal MET-1 and maintenance of that marking by maternal MES-4 are sufficient to maintain X repression in PGCs and promote germline survival.
source: These findings suggest that newly established H3K36me3 marking of H3K36me3(-) chromosomes by maternal MET-1 and maintenance of that marking by maternal MES-4 are sufficient to maintain X repression in PGCs and promote germline survival.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the genetic experiments showing that both MET-1 and MES-4 are required for germline development when H3K36me3(-) chromosomes are inherited.

claim: MES-4 levels are low on the X chromosome(s).
source: MES-4 levels are low on the X chromosome(s) (Bender et al., 2006; Rechtsteiner et al., 2010; Furuhashi et al., 2010; Gaydos et al., 2012; Kreher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LIN-15B targets the promoter of many X genes that are repressed by MES-4 in PGCs and/or EGCs.
source: First, our analysis of publicly available LIN-15B ChIP data from whole embryos and larvae found that LIN-15B targets the promoter of many X genes that are repressed by MES-4 in PGCs and/or EGCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of publicly available ChIP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: lin-15B is upregulated in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs.
source: Second, lin-15B is X-linked and UP in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and smFISH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: LIN-15B has been reported to promote expression of X genes in PGCs and adult germlines.
source: Third, LIN-15B has been reported to promote expression of X genes in PGCs and adult germlines (Lee et al., 2017; Robert et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: mes-4 and lin-15B genetically interact in somatic cells to control expression of germline genes such as genes encoding P-granule components.
source: Finally, mes-4 and lin-15B genetically interact in somatic cells to control expression of germline genes such as genes encoding P-granule components (Petrella et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- adult germlines upregulated considerably fewer X genes (112 X genes) than mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines (367 X genes).
source: Our differential expression analyses showed that mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- adult germlines upregulated considerably fewer X genes (112 X genes) than mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines (367 X genes) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The 367 X upregulated genes in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines had closer-to-wild-type transcript levels in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- adult germlines.
source: Furthermore, the 367 X UP genes in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines had closer-to-wild-type transcript levels in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- adult germlines (Figure 5B), and 323 of those X UP genes were scored as X DOWN genes in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- compared to mes-4 M+Z- (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: 323 of the 367 X upregulated genes in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines were scored as X downregulated genes in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- compared to mes-4 M+Z-.
source: Furthermore, the 367 X UP genes in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines had closer-to-wild-type transcript levels in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- adult germlines (Figure 5B), and 323 of those X UP genes were scored as X DOWN genes in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- compared to mes-4 M+Z- (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: LIN-15B is responsible for much of the X misexpression in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines.
source: Our results show that LIN-15B is responsible for much of the X misexpression in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that removal of LIN-15B reduces X misexpression in mes-4 mutants.

claim: Removal of either maternal LIN-15B, zygotic LIN-15B, or both increased the number of mes-4 M-Z- XspXsp offspring with a full-sized germline.
source: We found that removal of either maternal LIN-15B, zygotic LIN-15B, or both increased the number of mes-4 M-Z- XspXsp offspring with a full-sized germline (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Loss of maternal LIN-15B caused better recovery of germline health than loss of zygotic LIN-15B, and loss of both had an additive effect.
source: Notably, loss of maternal LIN-15B caused better recovery of germline health than loss of zygotic LIN-15B, and loss of both had an additive effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 88% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M-Z- XspXsp germlines were full-sized.
source: Strikingly, 88% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M-Z- XspXsp germlines were full-sized.
evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Both maternal and zygotic sources of the transcription factor LIN-15B contribute to germline loss in mes-4 M-Z- mutants.
source: We conclude that both maternal and zygotic sources of the transcription factor LIN-15B contribute to germline loss in mes-4 M-Z- mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments showing that removal of either maternal or zygotic LIN-15B improves germline health.

claim: 29% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M-Z- XooXsp adult mutant hermaphrodites made a full-sized germline compared to 0% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M+Z+ XooXsp adult mutant hermaphrodites.
source: We found that 29% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M-Z- XooXsp adult mutant hermaphrodites made a full-sized germline compared to 0% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M+Z+ XooXsp adult mutant hermaphrodites (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Removal of LIN-15B can allow mes-4 M-Z- XooXsp mutants to make a full-sized germline.
source: This finding demonstrates that removal of LIN-15B can even allow mes-4 M-Z- XooXsp mutants to make a full-sized germline.
evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only RNAi depletion of LIN-15B caused mes-4 M-Z- mutants to make a healthier germline among 20 candidate genes tested.
source: Of the 20 genes tested, only RNAi depletion of LIN-15B caused mes-4 M-Z- mutants to make a healthier germline (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: LIN-15B is a major contributor to germline death in mes-4 M-Z- mutants.
source: We conclude that LIN-15B is a major contributor to germline death in mes-4 M-Z- mutants.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that LIN-15B is the only factor among those tested whose depletion rescues germline health in mes-4 mutants.

claim: LIN-15B promotes expression of an oogenesis program in nanos mutant PGCs, which causes germline death in nanos mutants.
source: A previous study found that LIN-15B promotes expression of an oogenesis program in nanos mutant PGCs, which causes germline death in nanos mutants (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: 350 of the 584 X upregulated genes (60%) in mes-4 PGCs and/or EGCs are oogenesis genes, which is higher than expected by chance.
source: We found that 350 of the 584 X UP genes (60%) and 179 of the 712 autosomal UP genes (25%) are oogenesis genes, and that both proportions are higher than expected by chance (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: 179 of the 712 autosomal upregulated genes (25%) in mes-4 PGCs and/or EGCs are oogenesis genes, which is higher than expected by chance.
source: We found that 350 of the 584 X UP genes (60%) and 179 of the 712 autosomal UP genes (25%) are oogenesis genes, and that both proportions are higher than expected by chance (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: mes-4 nascent germlines misexpress an oogenesis program involving many X and autosomal genes, which may interfere with the ability of mutant PGCs to proliferate.
source: We conclude that mes-4 nascent germlines misexpress an oogenesis program involving many X and autosomal genes, which may interfere with the ability of mutant PGCs to proliferate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that oogenesis genes are enriched among upregulated genes in mes-4 nascent germlines.

claim: The sets of X upregulated genes and autosomal upregulated genes in mes-4 PGCs and/or EGCs are both enriched for LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes.
source: We found that our sets of X UP genes and autosomal UP genes in mes-4 PGCs and/or EGCs are both enriched for LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Almost all LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes on the X chromosome are upregulated in mes-4 (165 out of 192 genes, or 86%).
source: Strikingly, when considering just X genes, almost all LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes are UP in mes-4 (165 out of 192 genes, or 86%).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set overlap analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: 14% of LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes on autosomes are upregulated in mes-4 (67 out of 468 genes).
source: This percentage is much lower when considering just autosomal genes (67 out of 468 genes, or 14%).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set overlap analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: LIN-15B causes toxic misexpression of oogenesis genes, mainly X-linked oogenesis genes, in mes-4 nascent germlines, which ultimately causes those germlines to die.
source: We speculate that LIN-15B causes toxic misexpression of oogenesis genes, mainly X-linked oogenesis genes, in mes-4 nascent germlines, which ultimately causes those germlines to die.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the combined observations about LIN-15B, oogenesis genes, and germline death.

claim: The top two principal components in PCA captured 41% of the variance across all samples and clustered mes-4 and mes-3 mutant samples together by germline stage and away from wt samples.
source: In principal component analysis (PCA), the top two principal components captured 41% of the variance across all samples and clustered mes-4 and mes-3 mutant samples together by germline stage and away from wt samples (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 354 X genes were upregulated in mes-3 vs. wt PGCs.
source: Using differential expression analysis, we identified 354 X UP genes in mes-3 vs. wt PGCs and 443 X UP genes in mes-3 vs. wt EGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 443 X genes were upregulated in mes-3 vs. wt EGCs.
source: Using differential expression analysis, we identified 354 X UP genes in mes-3 vs. wt PGCs and 443 X UP genes in mes-3 vs. wt EGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Stage-matched mes-3 and mes-4 samples upregulated a highly similar set of X genes, many of which are oogenesis genes.
source: We found that stage-matched mes-3 and mes-4 samples upregulated a highly similar set of X genes, many of which are oogenesis genes (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7.

claim: There is a positive correlation (0.22 Spearman's correlation coefficient) between log2(fold change) of misregulated X genes in mes-4 and mes-3 PGCs.
source: We found a positive, albeit small, correlation between PGCs (0.22 Spearman's correlation coefficient) and a stronger correlation between EGCs (0.44 Spearman's correlation coefficient) (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There is a stronger positive correlation (0.44 Spearman's correlation coefficient) between log2(fold change) of misregulated X genes in mes-4 and mes-3 EGCs.
source: We found a positive, albeit small, correlation between PGCs (0.22 Spearman's correlation coefficient) and a stronger correlation between EGCs (0.44 Spearman's correlation coefficient) (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The correlation coefficient between mes-4 and mes-3 was higher when considering only X upregulated oogenesis genes.
source: For both comparisons, the correlation coefficient was higher when considering only X UP oogenesis genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Loss of LIN-15B caused mes-3 M-Z- mutants to make a healthier germline, as it does for mes-4 mutants.
source: Moreover, as in mes-4 M-Z- mutants, loss of LIN-15B caused mes-3 M-Z- mutants to make a healthier germline (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: mrg-1 PGCs misexpressed 440 X genes, 225 of which were also misexpressed in mes-4 and mes-3 PGCs and/or EGCs.
source: We found that mrg-1 PGCs misexpressed 440 X genes, 225 of which were also misexpressed in mes-4 and mes-3 PGCs and/or EGCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: met-1 M-Z- PGCs had only eight upregulated X genes.
source: We also profiled transcripts from PGCs hand-dissected from met-1 M-Z- L1 larvae, which lack the H3K36 HMT MET-1. We identified only eight upregulated X genes, which may explain why most met-1 worms are fertile when reared at normal growth temperature (20°C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Most met-1 worms are fertile when reared at normal growth temperature (20°C).
source: We also profiled transcripts from PGCs hand-dissected from met-1 M-Z- L1 larvae, which lack the H3K36 HMT MET-1. We identified only eight upregulated X genes, which may explain why most met-1 worms are fertile when reared at normal growth temperature (20°C).
evidence: This is stated as a known observation.

claim: MRG-1 is added to the team of maternal regulators that ensure PGC survival and health by repressing the X.
source: Our extended transcriptome analysis adds MRG-1 to the team of maternal regulators that ensure PGC survival and health by repressing the X.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mrg-1 mutants misexpress X genes similarly to mes-4 and mes-3 mutants.

claim: Nascent C. elegans germlines that completely lack maternal MES-4 misexpress over 1000 genes, most of which are on the X chromosome.
source: We found that nascent C. elegans germlines (PGCs and EGCs) that completely lack maternal MES-4 misexpress over 1000 genes, most of which are on the X chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Maternal MES-4 promotes offspring germline development by preventing LIN-15B from activating a germline-toxic program of gene expression from the X chromosome, a program that is normally activated during oogenesis in hermaphrodites.
source: We favor a model where maternal MES-4 promotes offspring germline development by preventing LIN-15B from activating a germline-toxic program of gene expression from the X chromosome, a program that is normally activated during oogenesis in hermaphrodites (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined findings from the study.

claim: The hand-dissection strategy offers advantages over FACS because FACS often does not yield pure samples, takes several hours to perform, and requires large numbers of worms.
source: This strategy offers numerous advantages over the popular cell isolation strategy, fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), because FACS often (1) does not yield pure samples, (2) takes several hours to perform, during which time sample integrity may decline, and (3) requires large numbers of worms, which may be hard to obtain for some mutants, like mes-4 mutants.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about FACS limitations.

claim: MES-4 is not required for PGCs to launch a germline program.
source: Furthermore, our genetic findings show that mes-4 mutants can develop a full-sized germline if they inherit X chromosomes that have a history of repression, demonstrating that MES-4 is not required for PGCs to launch a germline program.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that some mes-4 mutants can develop full germlines under specific conditions.

claim: MES-4 is required for the misexpression of germline genes in somatic tissues of several mutants, such as spr-5; met-2, lin-15B, and mutants of DREAM complex components.
source: Interestingly, MES-4 is required for the misexpression of germline genes in somatic tissues of several mutants, such as spr-5; met-2, lin-15B, and mutants of DREAM complex components (Wang et al., 2005; Petrella et al., 2011; Carpenter et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Maternal MES-4 has tissue-dependent roles in gene regulation.
source: This suggests that maternal MES-4 has tissue-dependent roles in gene regulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MES-4 has different effects in germline vs. somatic tissues.

claim: Context-dependent roles of MES-4 may be mediated by different H3K36me3 'reader' complexes, as observed in other organisms.
source: Such context-dependent roles may be mediated by different H3K36me3 'reader' complexes, as observed in other organisms (Yochum and Ayer, 2002; Cai et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to studies in other organisms.

claim: Inheritance of H3K36me3 patterns from parents is not required for offspring germline development.
source: By taking advantage of the gpr-1 genetic tool, we demonstrated that inheritance of H3K36me3 patterns from parents is not required for offspring germline development.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments using the gpr-1 tool.

claim: Maternal MES-4 and maternal MET-1 perform cooperative, but distinct, roles to restore sufficient levels and proper patterns of H3K36me3 marking to chromosomes inherited lacking H3K36me3.
source: We speculate that maternal MES-4 and maternal MET-1 perform cooperative, but distinct, roles to restore sufficient levels and proper patterns of H3K36me3 marking to chromosomes inherited lacking H3K36me3, to allow germline development.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on genetic experiments.

claim: Maternal MET-1 first catalyzes new H3K36me3 marking on genes co-transcriptionally during the first wave of zygotic genome activation in embryonic PGCs, after which maternal MES-4 maintains MET-1-generated patterns of H3K36me3 through early germline development.
source: In this scenario, we envision that maternal MET-1 first catalyzes new H3K36me3 marking on genes co-transcriptionally during the first wave of zygotic genome activation in embryonic PGCs, after which maternal MES-4 maintains MET-1-generated patterns of H3K36me3 through early germline development (Furuhashi et al., 2010; Kreher et al., 2018) to repress X genes and prevent germline death.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on genetic experiments and citations to previous studies.

claim: De novo H3K36me3 marking on autosomes likely indirectly causes X repression in PGCs since most X genes are not transcribed in PGCs and therefore do not get de novo marked with H3K36me3.
source: De novo H3K36me3 marking on autosomes likely indirectly causes X repression in PGCs since most X genes are not transcribed in PGCs and therefore do not get de novo marked with H3K36me3.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from known biology.

claim: Loss of the candidate H3K36me3 'reader' MRG-1 causes PGCs to misexpress a set of X genes similar to that caused by loss MES-4 and also causes death of the nascent germline.
source: The importance of H3K36me3 marking is also highlighted by our finding that loss of the candidate H3K36me3 'reader' MRG-1 (homolog of yeast Eaf-3, fly MSL3, and human MRG15) (Gorman et al., 1995; Eisen et al., 2001; Cai et al., 2003; Bertram and Pereira-Smith, 2001; Joshi and Struhl, 2005) causes PGCs to misexpress a set of X genes similar to that caused by loss MES-4 and also causes death of the nascent germline.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to previous studies.

claim: met-1 M-Z- worms are fertile when reared at standard 20°C growth temperature.
source: met-1 M-Z- worms are fertile when reared at standard 20°C growth temperature (Andersen and Horvitz, 2007), and met-1 M-Z- PGCs misexpress very few genes (this study).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In met-1 mutant embryos maternal MES-4 can propagate patterns of pre-existing H3K36me3 inherited from parents to PGCs.
source: One explanation is that in met-1 mutant embryos maternal MES-4 can propagate patterns of pre-existing H3K36me3 inherited from parents to PGCs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why met-1 mutants are fertile.

claim: Maternal MET-1's role in de novo H3K36me3 marking in response to transcriptional turn-on is not required so long as genes were pre-marked with H3K36me3 in parents.
source: This predicts that maternal MET-1's role in de novo H3K36me3 marking in response to transcriptional turn-on is not required so long as genes were pre-marked with H3K36me3 in parents.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the observation that met-1 mutants are fertile.

claim: In the absence of MET-1 function, maternal MES-4 may be able to faithfully transmit pre-existing patterns of H3K36me3 across generations and through development indefinitely.
source: This scenario raises the fascinating possibility that in the absence of MET-1 function, maternal MES-4 may be able to faithfully transmit pre-existing patterns of H3K36me3 across generations and through development indefinitely.
evidence: This is a speculative possibility based on the observation that met-1 mutants are fertile.

claim: MES-4 likely regulates expression of X genes indirectly in PGCs.
source: Since MES-4 binding and its HMT activity are very low across almost the entire X chromosome (Rechtsteiner et al., 2010), it is likely that MES-4 regulates expression of X genes indirectly in PGCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MES-4 has low activity on the X chromosome.

claim: One possible mechanism for indirect regulation is that MES-4 generates H3K36me3 on autosomes to repel and concentrate a transcriptional repressor on the X chromosome(s).
source: One possible mechanism for indirect regulation is that MES-4 generates H3K36me3 on autosomes to repel and concentrate a transcriptional repressor on the X chromosome(s).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: PRC2 is an attractive candidate repressor that may be concentrated on the X chromosome(s) by MES-4 activity on autosomes.
source: An attractive candidate repressor is the H3K27 HMT PRC2: in germlines, PRC2 activity is concentrated on the X chromosome(s) (Bender et al., 2004), PRC2 represses a highly similar set of X genes as MES-4 (Gaydos et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2017; this study), and loss of PRC2 causes maternal-effect sterility, like loss of MES-4 (Capowski et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and data from this study.

claim: H3K36me3's role in antagonizing methylation of H3K27 is well documented.
source: H3K36me3's role in antagonizing methylation of H3K27 is well documented (Schmitges et al., 2011; Yuan et al., 2011; Gaydos et al., 2012; Evans et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: H3K36me3 in germlines may sequester a transcriptional activator on autosomes and away from the X chromosome(s) as it does to the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) CBP-1 in C. elegans intestinal cells.
source: An alternative possibility is that H3K36me3 in germlines sequesters a transcriptional activator on autosomes and away from the X chromosome(s) as it does to the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) CBP-1 in C. elegans intestinal cells (Cabianca et al., 2019; Georgescu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to previous studies in intestinal cells.

claim: Upregulation of lin-15B also causes sterility in nanos mutants and set-2 (H3K4 HMT) mutants and leads to upregulation of other X genes.
source: Recent studies found that upregulation of lin-15B also causes sterility in nanos mutants and set-2 (H3K4 HMT) mutants and leads to upregulation of other X genes (Lee et al., 2017; Robert et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The germline uses multiple protective mechanisms to antagonize LIN-15B.
source: Those findings coupled with ours suggest that excessive LIN-15B activity causes germline-toxic levels of X-chromosome expression and that the germline uses multiple protective mechanisms to antagonize LIN-15B.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that multiple mutants (nanos, set-2, mes-4) show similar effects related to LIN-15B.

claim: LIN-15B promotes repressive H3K9me2 marking in the promoter of germline-specific genes in somatic cells.
source: Recently, LIN-15B was shown to promote repressive H3K9me2 marking in the promoter of germline-specific genes in somatic cells (Rechtsteiner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: LIN-15B may activate expression of X genes indirectly, for example, by downregulating or antagonizing a repressor of X genes.
source: In germlines, LIN-15B may activate expression of X genes indirectly, for example, by downregulating or antagonizing a repressor of X genes.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: LIN-15B may have context-dependent roles in gene expression and may directly activate expression of X genes.
source: Alternatively, LIN-15B may have context-dependent roles in gene expression, a well-known feature of many transcription factors (Fry and Farnham, 1999), and may directly activate expression of X genes.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation to a previous study about transcription factors.

claim: LIN-15B is associated with the promoter of many X genes that are upregulated in mes-4 nascent germlines.
source: In support of this model, our analysis of LIN-15B ChIP data from whole embryos and larvae found that LIN-15B is associated with the promoter of many X genes that are upregulated in mes-4 nascent germlines.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of publicly available ChIP data.

claim: The fertility of mes-4 mutant worms is less dependent on the absolute number of X chromosomes in the germline than on whether the X(s) was inherited from the oocyte or sperm.
source: Notably, the fertility of mes-4 mutant worms is less dependent on the absolute number of X chromosomes in the germline than on whether the X(s) was inherited from the oocyte or sperm: 1X germlines with an Xoo are typically sterile while 1X germlines with an Xsp are typically fertile, and 2X germlines with one or two Xoo are sterile while 2X germlines with two Xsp can be fertile.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments analyzing different X-chromosome inheritance patterns.

claim: MES-4 and PRC2 prevent misexpression of an oogenesis program, which is enriched for genes on the X.
source: Instead of MES-4 and PRC2 performing X-dosage compensation, we favor the view that they prevent misexpression of an oogenesis program, which is enriched for genes on the X (Ortiz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined findings from the study.

claim: 60% of X genes upregulated in mutant PGCs and/or EGCs are oogenesis genes.
source: First, 60% of X genes upregulated in mutant PGCs and/or EGCs are oogenesis genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis.

claim: LIN-15B is an oogenesis gene and binds to the promoters of many other X-linked oogenesis genes.
source: Second, LIN-15B, a key X target of MES-4 and PRC2 repression, is an oogenesis gene and binds to the promoters of many other X-linked oogenesis genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set analysis and ChIP data analysis.

claim: Upregulation of LIN-15B in nanos mutant germlines causes misexpression of oogenesis genes and death of nascent germ cells.
source: Third, upregulation of LIN-15B in nanos mutant germlines causes misexpression of oogenesis genes and death of nascent germ cells (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The oocyte-inherited X chromosome has a history of expression of oogenesis genes and may be prone to turning those genes on in nascent germ cells in offspring that lack MES-4 or PRC2.
source: Since the oocyte-inherited X chromosome has a history of expression of oogenesis genes, it may be prone to turning those genes on in, and thereby causing death of, nascent germ cells in offspring that lack MES-4 or PRC2.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the observation that X-chromosome inheritance pattern affects germline health.

claim: Offspring germ cells that lack MES-4 or PRC2 can develop into full-sized germlines if they inherit only X chromosomes from sperm, which were not turned on for oogenesis and have a history of repression.
source: In support of this, offspring germ cells that lack MES-4 or PRC2 can develop into full-sized germlines if they inherit only X chromosomes from sperm, which were not turned on for oogenesis and have a history of repression.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments.

claim: MES-4 and PRC2 protect germline survival and proliferation by silencing an X-linked oogenesis program that may interfere with the developmental fate of nascent germ cells.
source: Together, our findings support a model where MES-4 and PRC2 protect germline survival and proliferation by silencing an X-linked oogenesis program that may interfere with the developmental fate of nascent germ cells.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined findings from the study.

claim: C. elegans germ granules (aka P granules) protect germline fate but are not needed to specify it.
source: Several studies demonstrated that C. elegans germ granules (aka P granules) protect germline fate but are not needed to specify it (Gallo et al., 2010; Updike et al., 2014; Knutson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 22G small RNAs are bound by the argonaute CSR-1 and have been shown to target most germline-expressed genes and promote expression of some.
source: They are bound by the argonaute CSR-1 and have been shown to target most germline-expressed genes and promote expression of some (Claycomb et al., 2009; Conine et al., 2010; Wedeles and Claycomb, 2013; Cecere et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Complete loss of CSR-1 or DRH-3 causes sterility.
source: Complete loss of CSR-1 or DRH-3, an RNA helicase that generates 22G RNAs, causes sterility (Duchaine et al., 2006; Claycomb et al., 2009; Gu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hypomorphic mutations in the helicase domain of DRH-3 that abolish production of most 22G RNAs do not impact germline formation.
source: However, hypomorphic mutations in the helicase domain of DRH-3 that abolish production of most 22G RNAs do not impact germline formation, suggesting that 22G RNAs are not needed to specify germline fate (Gu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In C. elegans germline fate may be the default, which must be protected in the germline and opposed in somatic tissues.
source: We propose the intriguing possibility that in C. elegans germline fate is the default, which must be protected in the germline (e.g., by MES proteins and P granules) and opposed in somatic tissues (e.g., by DREAM and LIN-15B).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the combined findings from the study.
